figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Illustration of the OpenVoice framework. We use a base speaker model to control the styles and languages, and a converter to embody the tone color of the reference speaker into the speech.
figures.headline: The framework pairs a base speaker model for style and language with a converter that applies the reference tone color.

abstract: We introduce OpenVoice, a versatile instant voice cloning approach that requires only a short audio clip from the reference speaker to replicate their voice and generate speech in multiple languages. OpenVoice represents a significant advancement in addressing the following open challenges in the field: 1) Flexible Voice Style Control. OpenVoice enables granular control over voice styles, including emotion, accent, rhythm, pauses, and intonation, in addition to replicating the tone color of the reference speaker. The voice styles are not directly copied from and constrained by the style of the reference speaker. Previous approaches lacked the ability to flexibly manipulate voice styles after cloning. 2) Zero-Shot Cross-Lingual Voice Cloning. OpenVoice achieves zero-shot cross-lingual voice cloning for languages not included in the massive-speaker training set. Unlike previous approaches, which typically require extensive massive-speaker multi-lingual (MSML) dataset for all languages, OpenVoice can clone voices into a new language without any massive-speaker training data for that language. OpenVoice is also computationally efficient, costing tens of times less than commercially available APIs that offer even inferior performance. To foster further research in the field, we have made the source code and trained model publicly accessible. We also provide qualitative results in our demo website. OpenVoice has served more than 2M users worldwide as the voice engine of MyShell.ai.

sections.body: The introduction defines instant voice cloning (IVC) as cloning a reference speaker's voice from a short audio sample without training on that speaker. It reviews autoregressive models such as VALLE and XTTS, which clone tone color but do not allow manipulation of emotion, accent, rhythm, pauses or intonation, and which are computationally expensive and slow. Non-autoregressive models such as YourTTS and Voicebox run faster but still lack style control. Existing methods typically need a large MSML dataset for cross-lingual cloning. The authors state that OpenVoice targets style control, zero-shot cross-lingual cloning and fast inference. They report that the internal version was used tens of millions of times between May and October 2023, and that source code and model weights are public.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Instant voice cloning needs a short reference clip, but existing methods lack style control and multi-language cloning without large multi-speaker data.

sections.body: The base speaker TTS model, by default a modified VITS, takes language, style and emotion embeddings and produces speech. The tone color converter is an encoder-decoder with an invertible normalizing flow in between. The flow layers map features to a representation that removes tone color but keeps other styles, trained by minimizing KL-divergence against phoneme features aligned with dynamic time warping. Running the flow in reverse with the reference tone color embedding adds that tone color back, and HiFi-GAN decodes the waveform. The model is feed-forward. The base model was trained on 30K sentences from two English speakers, one Chinese speaker and one Japanese speaker. The converter was trained on 300K samples from 20K individuals. The authors state that the submodules are borrowed from prior work, and that the contribution is the decoupled framework.
sections.heading: Approach
sections.headline: OpenVoice decouples a base speaker text-to-speech model for style and language from a tone color converter that adds the reference voice.

sections.body: The authors argue that numerical comparison with prior work is unfair because training and test sets differ, so they report qualitative results and publish audio samples. Tone color cloning was tested on reference speakers from celebrities, game characters and anonymous individuals, with any of four base speakers. For style control, 1K samples with diverse styles were generated from the base model and Microsoft TTS, and the authors report that styles are well preserved. In rare cases emotion was slightly neutralized, which they reduced by averaging tone color embeddings. Cross-lingual cloning works for an unseen language without massive-speaker data when a base speaker exists. A slightly optimized version reaches $12\times$ real-time on a single A10G GPU, or 85ms per second of speech, with an estimated upper bound of $40\times$. IPA phonemes were found crucial for cross-lingual cloning; other phoneme dictionaries produced non-native output.
sections.heading: Experiment
sections.headline: OpenVoice is evaluated qualitatively rather than against baselines, reaching 12 times real-time speed on one graphics processing unit.

sections.body: The discussion restates the approach: a base speaker text-to-speech model controls voice styles and languages, and a separate converter handles tone color. The authors state that this makes OpenVoice more flexible than previous approaches in voice styles and languages. They describe the decoupling as the foundational design principle. The section reports no new experiments. Source code and model weights are made publicly available to support future research.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: Decoupling tone color from style and language is presented as the core principle, with code and weights released.
